summary: The state's second investigative body in the fortnight, announced 31 July and reported 1 August. A three-member Safety and Compliance Audit Team under a former MARAD Director-General, Dr Ivor English, with Col. Julius Skeete of the GDF and Capt. Joseph Lewis. Its remit is prospective — compliance standards for marine vessels generally, rather than the Barima — and, like the Commission before it, it arrives with no deadline, no budget, no terms of reference published as a document, and no undertaking to publish. It is established by presidential directive with no statutory basis stated, and nothing in the report says how it relates to the Commission of Inquiry.

The second source on the Safety and Compliance Audit Team, published the same day as Kaieteur News and naming the same three members, which takes the appointment out of single-source territory. It carries the fuller quotation of the remit — oversight, enforcement, and "the highest practicable standards of safety and accountability" — and gives the toll as 73 dead and 30 missing from 179, which matters because it is the outlet closest to the administration carrying 73 while the government's own information service carried 72 on 30 July.

The first time the opposition leader has put the charging decision in these terms: that the three charged employees are being scapegoated to shield ministers. Norton calls the charges "ridiculous, vindictive, and intended to silence the workers" and moves the question up the chain — who allowed the vessel to sail, who certified it, who supervised its maintenance. Two things in it are new to this corpus: the demand that the state say which ministries owned the cargo aboard, and the allegation that pre-departure inspection procedures broke down. Both are single-source. The piece also repeats a characterisation of the DPP's statement that this archive has already recorded as the reporting outlet's wording and not a quotation of her, and it is flagged rather than carried.

The first sustained published argument on the government's side of the question this archive has recorded as unanswered since 28 July: whether the Commission of Inquiry and the murder prosecution can properly run together. The column separates their purposes — systemic fact-finding against individual guilt — and makes one claim that matters more than the rest, that the Commissions of Inquiry Act already contains provisions protecting witnesses from self-incrimination, and that Parliament therefore contemplated exactly this overlap. That is a columnist's reading of a statute this archive does not hold, marked single-source; if it is right, it is the answer nobody in government has given. It also brings the 2014 MV Sewol disaster into the corpus as precedent for parallel proceedings.

The first report that the President has committed to attempting a salvage, and it moves the state's position materially: every prior statement in this corpus either left the decision with the families or had the Prime Minister saying the wreck was likely to remain where it is. Relatives of three missing Berbicians say they were told at a meeting on 29 July that a lift could take eight to ten weeks. It is single-source, reaches the archive through families' accounts of a private meeting, and no government release confirms either the commitment or the timeframe. Recorded as a development in the state's position and not as a decision, because nothing published by the state says so.

The practical end of the recovery operation: the Prime Minister confirms diving has ceased and the French Guiana Army, Trinidad and Tobago Coast Guard and Brazilian Navy teams have left the country, with the 18-asset deployment scaled back to patrol boats and daily aerial surveillance. About thirty people were never recovered. On the wreck he restates the position this archive has recorded throughout — the government is weighing salvage against a memorial and will be guided by the families — which sits alongside, and does not confirm, the same day's report that the President has committed to attempting a lift. The piece also dates the swearing-in of the Commission to 31 July, against 30 July everywhere else including the state's own release; recorded as a reporting error.

A release this archive missed on the day and which materially narrows one of its standing gaps. The GDF Chief of Staff announces an after-action review of the search and rescue operation whose stated scope is precisely the material this site has repeatedly recorded as unpublished: communications between the control tower, the lighthouse, the Search and Rescue Coordination Centre and Coast Guard operations, from the distress signal to the end of the mission. It establishes that such a record exists and is to be analysed, which is different from the absence the archive had recorded. What it does not establish is that anyone outside the GDF will see it: the release sets no deadline, names no recipient, and gives no undertaking to publish.

A government release of 28 July that this archive did not hold, and which matters for two reasons. It gives the state's own figures on that date — 73 recovered, 68 identified, five awaiting identification, 30 unaccounted for, 76 survivors — so the 73 that the Department of Public Information itself abandoned without explanation on 30 July was its own published figure two days earlier. And it confirms the operational picture at that point: 18 assets, three aircraft and 15 vessels, from Waini Point to Adventure. Like every other state statement here it reports the recovered and the unaccounted for and never adds them together.

A state release of 28 July carrying the first first-hand account in this corpus of conditions at the wreck from the diving side: a Trinidad and Tobago Coast Guard officer describing visibility of under a foot, strong tidal currents at the river mouth and shallow water defeating visual search. It matters to the wreck question because these are the conditions later relied on, and it is the state's own account of them. It also carries an asset count of 17 — 14 vessels and three aircraft — against 18 in the Prime Minister's release of the same day, a small unreconciled divergence between two government releases published hours apart.

The state's own profile of Commissioner Hamada Fouda, published 26 July and not previously held here: 35 years in marine regulation and casualty investigation, Senior Maritime Surveyor for Jamaica's maritime authority since 2011, leading casualty investigations under the IMO Casualty Investigation Code since 2019. It is relevant beyond biography because Kiskadee Watch put conflict-of-interest questions about this commissioner to three government bodies on 31 July and received no reply from any of them; this release is what the state has said about him, and it speaks to qualification rather than to interest.
